In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the speed of a high speed train is determined by the following factors: the adhesion between the wheel and the rail, the geometry of the wheel-rail contact, the inertia of the bogie and the frame, and the stiffness of the suspension.

, for high-speed trains, the critical speed is a function of: the primary suspension stiffness, the wheel-rail contact geometry, the bogie and body inertia, the secondary suspension characteristics and the wheel-rail friction.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we are able to demonstrate that the maximum speed of railway vehicles with solid axles is limited mainly by the properties of wheel-rail contact geometry, by the creep forces, and by the inertial properties of the bogie and the car body.
the critical speed of a railway vehicle is a function of the primary suspension stiffness, the wheel/rail contact geometry and the secondary suspension design.

the critical velocity of a railway vehicle is a function, primarily, of the stiffness of the primary suspension, the geometry of the wheel-rail contact, the inertial properties of the bogie and the car, and the design of the secondary suspension.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the maximum critical speed for a given vehicle is limited by the wheel-rail geometry and by creep coefficients, and that the suspension can only improve the critical speed by a limited amount.
the maximum critical speed is severely limited by the characteristics of the wheel-rail contact.

the maximum critical speed of a high-speed railway vehicle with a solid axle bogie is mainly a function of the primary suspension stiffness, the wheel-rail contact geometry and properties, the bogie and car inertial properties and the secondary suspension design (conicity can vary in the practice between 0.05 and 0.3, and the creep stiffness can be 25 to 100% of the predicted values by Kalker).
